Collected full article body: SATURDAY MORNING WITH CRANKY DON JOE | Artificial Intelligence Is Supposed to Make Life Easier. So Why Is Everybody Worried About Losing Their Jobs?

By Cranky Don Joe

My name is Cranky Don Joe. Cranky DJ to a lot of my neighbors. I am not an expert on artificial intelligence, which immediately puts me ahead of Larry, because I am willing to admit that I don't know whether computers are going to take everybody's jobs.

Larry watched a forty-minute webinar on Tuesday and has been explaining the future of human employment ever since. By Thursday, he was recommending that I embrace automation, learn three new skills, and prepare for a world in which machines do most of the work. I asked him who would be paying my electric bill in this wonderful new world. He told me I was resisting progress.

I have nothing against progress. I like my microwave oven, my washing machine, and the fact that I no longer have to stand beside a television twisting an antenna until the evening news stops looking like a snowstorm. I appreciate technology that saves me time. What I don't understand is why every new invention arrives with a promise to make my life easier and a set of instructions explaining how much more work I must do before I can enjoy the convenience. The television needs a software update, the refrigerator wants to connect to the internet, and my printer has developed the habit of refusing to print until I acknowledge a message about a service I never requested. I bought the printer because I wanted something printed; apparently, that was an unreasonable expectation.

Artificial intelligence has taken this arrangement to a whole new level. People tell me it can write letters, organize schedules, analyze documents, prepare presentations, answer customer questions, and perform tasks that once kept entire offices busy. Some employers are looking for ways to use it to reduce costs, and some workers are worried about what that means for their jobs. Others are discovering that the technology can take tedious work off their hands and give them more time for things that require actual human judgment. I can understand why people are interested. I can also understand why somebody who has spent twenty years becoming good at a profession might feel uneasy when a company announces that a computer can now perform part of that profession before lunch.

Larry, naturally, considers the entire development tremendously exciting.

He arrived at my house shortly after nine on Saturday morning carrying his laptop, a travel mug, and a notebook labeled AI TRANSFORMATION STRATEGY. He had made the label himself. Larry has always believed that a project becomes more important once it has a title printed in capital letters.

"Don, we're living through a technological revolution," he announced. I told him I was trying to live through breakfast.

He sat at my kitchen table without waiting to be invited and opened his laptop. He wanted to demonstrate how artificial intelligence could improve my daily routine. I asked whether the demonstration would require creating an account, downloading an application, or giving somebody permission to collect information about me.

"Not necessarily," he said.

I have known Larry long enough to understand that this was not a reassuring answer.

He explained that the real advantage of AI was productivity: tasks that once required hours could now be completed in minutes. Businesses could operate more efficiently, employees could concentrate on higher-value responsibilities, and people like me could spend less time dealing with routine obligations.

I asked whether he had used the technology to finish cleaning his garage.

"That's different." "Why?" "Because the garage requires physical labor." "So does taking out the trash, Larry. Has artificial intelligence figured that out?"

He said robotics would eventually address many physical tasks as well. I asked whether the robots would also return borrowed extension cords. Larry looked up from his laptop and reminded me that he had already returned mine after Halloween. I told him I was pleased he remembered, because I had begun to suspect the cord had entered a long-term research program.

Larry said I was missing the larger point: the technology was not intended simply to replace people; it could help them become more productive.

That sounded reasonable enough, so I asked him to explain what would happen if a company discovered that ten employees could now accomplish the work previously performed by fifteen.

He said the company might expand its operations, develop new services, or assign those employees to more valuable work.

"Or it might decide it only needs ten employees," I said. He admitted that was possible. "What happens to the other five?" "They may need to retrain." "For what?" "New opportunities." "What new opportunities?"

He paused, took a drink of coffee, and told me the labor market was evolving.

I asked whether the labor market had informed the five employees where they were supposed to report on Monday morning. Larry said I was oversimplifying a complicated economic transition. I agreed that it was complicated, particularly for the people whose rent was due while everybody else discussed the transition.

He decided a practical demonstration would be more useful than an argument. He opened an AI assistant and announced that we would begin by improving my household efficiency.

His first suggestion was to create a weekly meal plan. I told him I already had one: I ate what was in the refrigerator, and when there was nothing left, I went to the grocery store. Larry said that approach lacked structure. He typed a request for a nutritious, economical seven-day meal plan for a retired man living in Minnesota.

The computer produced an elaborate schedule containing breakfast, lunch, dinner, snacks, and a detailed shopping list. Larry read it aloud with the enthusiasm of a man announcing a major scientific discovery: Monday's breakfast involved Greek yogurt, chia seeds, blueberries, and something called overnight oats; Tuesday included quinoa; Wednesday required fresh salmon; and by Thursday, I was expected to prepare a vegetable dish containing ingredients I had never purchased and could not confidently pronounce.

I asked how much the groceries would cost. Larry entered another request. The computer estimated a budget, and he explained that the total would vary depending on local prices and store availability.

I told him my usual breakfast was two eggs and toast.

"That's not the point, Don." "Then what is the point?" "The system is helping you make informed decisions." "I was already informed, Larry. I knew I wanted eggs."

He suggested that we could customize the plan to reflect my preferences. I asked whether we could customize it until it told me to eat the eggs I already owned. He typed several more instructions, reviewed the revised schedule, and finally announced that the computer recommended two eggs and toast for breakfast.

We had spent twenty minutes discovering what I had known when he walked through the door. Larry called that personalization; I called it Saturday morning.

His next demonstration involved composing a message to Helen. He explained that AI could help people communicate more clearly, especially when discussing difficult subjects. I asked what difficult subject he needed to discuss with his wife.

He said he had promised to repair a loose cabinet handle in their kitchen and had not yet found the time. Helen had reminded him about it several times, and he wanted to send a thoughtful message acknowledging the delay.

I suggested he fix the handle.

Larry said communication was an important part of maintaining a healthy relationship. I agreed, but I thought a screwdriver might be more effective in this particular situation.

He typed a request for a warm, professional message apologizing to his wife for failing to complete a household repair. The computer produced several paragraphs expressing appreciation for Helen's patience, acknowledging the inconvenience, and committing to a realistic timeline for resolving the issue.

Larry read the message carefully. "That's actually very good," he said. I asked whether he intended to send it. "With a few adjustments."

I told him Helen had been married to him long enough to recognize when he had suddenly begun communicating like the human resources department of a large insurance company. He ignored me and sent a shortened version.

A few minutes later, his phone rang. It was Helen. I could hear her without the speakerphone.

"Larry, did you use that computer thing to write me a letter about the cabinet?" He looked at me. "Well, I used it to help organize my thoughts." "Your thoughts about a cabinet handle?" "I wanted to acknowledge your concerns." "Larry, my concern is that the handle is still loose."

He tried to explain that the message represented a commitment to action. Helen told him that if he had enough time to compose a formal apology, he had enough time to walk into the garage, get the screwdriver, and repair the cabinet. Then she asked whether the computer had provided a completion date.

Larry admitted that it had suggested one. "What date?" "Next Tuesday." "Wonderful. Tell the computer I expect the handle fixed by noon."

She hung up.

Larry stared at the phone for several seconds before closing the messaging window. I asked whether the artificial intelligence had improved his communication. He said Helen had misunderstood the intention, but I told him she had understood it perfectly: she wanted the cabinet fixed.

About that time, Frank came over carrying a small package he had received by mistake. The delivery driver had left it at his house instead of mine. Frank noticed Larry's laptop and asked whether we were working on something.

Larry explained that he was demonstrating the benefits of artificial intelligence. Frank pulled out a chair.

"Good. Ask it why the Vikings keep breaking my heart."

Larry said the technology could analyze sports statistics, but he doubted it could answer a question that subjective. Frank told him that was disappointing; he had been hoping for a breakthrough.

Then Larry began describing how AI might transform the workplace. Frank listened for a while before asking whether companies were really going to replace employees with computers.

Larry said some jobs would change, some tasks would be automated, and new occupations would emerge. He explained that technological change had always affected employment, from agricultural machinery to factory automation and personal computers.

Frank agreed that new technology had created jobs in the past, but he also pointed out that people who lost their jobs during those transitions did not necessarily become the people hired for the new ones.

"My cousin worked in a warehouse for twenty-three years," Frank said. "When they brought in new equipment, everybody talked about efficiency. My cousin still had to find another job. Efficiency didn't pay his mortgage."

Larry acknowledged that workers could face difficult transitions, and said training and education would be important.

Frank asked whether the companies benefiting from automation would help pay for that training. Larry said that depended on the employer.

"And while somebody's being trained, who's paying the bills?" Larry admitted that was an important policy question.

Frank looked at me. "Every time I ask him where the money comes from, it becomes a policy question."

I told Frank that was how Larry's explanations worked: as long as we discussed productivity, the future looked wonderful; the moment somebody mentioned groceries, rent, or health insurance, we had apparently wandered into advanced economics.

Larry objected that artificial intelligence could create opportunities for entrepreneurs and small businesses. He said somebody running a one-person operation might use it to prepare invoices, develop marketing materials, answer routine questions, and compete with larger organizations.

That was a fair point, and I told him so. A small business owner who spends evenings sorting paperwork might welcome a tool that gives back a few hours; a teacher preparing classroom materials might find it useful; and a mechanic might benefit from faster access to technical information, provided the information is accurate. Technology can be valuable without becoming the answer to every problem.

Larry appeared relieved that I had finally said something favorable.

Then Frank asked whether the computer could run a neighborhood association meeting. Larry said it could help prepare an agenda, summarize discussions, and organize action items. Frank wanted to know whether it could stop Larry from talking after the meeting was supposed to end, and I told him that might require a more advanced system.

Larry decided we were not taking the demonstration seriously enough. He opened another window and asked the AI assistant to prepare a Saturday schedule that would maximize his productivity while allowing time for household chores, exercise, professional development, and relaxation.

The computer produced a detailed itinerary beginning at seven in the morning. It included thirty minutes of stretching, forty-five minutes of reading, a structured breakfast, a household maintenance period, a learning session, a neighborhood engagement activity, and several short breaks.

Frank examined the schedule. "Where's lunch?" Larry pointed to a thirty-minute block. "Where's your nap?" "I don't usually take a nap." "Maybe that's your problem."

I noticed that the schedule included a forty-five-minute period for professional development and asked what profession Larry was developing. He explained that he was exploring opportunities in AI consulting.

Frank looked interested. "Consulting on what?" "Helping people adopt artificial intelligence." "How long have you been using it?" "Several months."

Frank considered that. "So you're going to charge people to explain something you're still learning?" Larry said consultants were expected to continue learning throughout their careers.

I told Frank that Larry had already been consulting for free around the neighborhood for years: he had advised us about snow removal, lawn maintenance, recycling, emergency preparedness, and Halloween safety. Charging for it might be the only thing he hadn't tried.

Larry said I was being unfair; he had valuable organizational experience. Frank reminded him about the Halloween incident when he had appointed himself safety director and ended up being frightened by a remote-controlled spider. Larry said that had been an isolated equipment problem, but I pointed out that the equipment had belonged to a child and that the child had operated it considerably more successfully than Larry had operated his entire haunted garage.

Larry closed the scheduling window. He was beginning to lose confidence in his audience.

That afternoon, he decided to test the technology on a genuine neighborhood problem. The association was looking for volunteers to help coordinate its winter preparedness meeting, and Larry wanted to submit a proposal. He asked the AI assistant to draft an application describing his leadership experience, community involvement, organizational skills, and commitment to public safety.

Within seconds, the computer produced a polished statement presenting Larry as an experienced community leader with a strong record of coordinating neighborhood initiatives. He read it aloud. Frank listened with growing interest.

"Who is that fellow?" "Me," Larry said. "Are you sure?"

The application referred to Larry's experience managing public safety initiatives, developing community preparedness strategies, and overseeing seasonal neighborhood operations. It sounded impressive, although I recognized several activities that had consisted mainly of Larry printing instructions and trying to persuade unwilling neighbors to follow them.

I asked whether the statement accurately described what he had done. Larry said it reflected his experience in professional language. I reminded him that his Halloween safety operation had never been authorized by the neighborhood association. He said that did not diminish the planning involved.

Frank asked whether the computer had included the spider incident. Larry said it had not.

"Then the application is incomplete," Frank told him.

Larry revised the statement to remove some of the grander claims. I thought that was sensible: there was nothing wrong with using technology to improve the wording of an application, but the person submitting it still had to make sure the facts were correct. A computer could make Larry sound like the director of a statewide emergency management agency, but it could not make his neighbors forget that he had once measured the distance between a plastic tombstone and Frank's sidewalk.

By late afternoon, Helen called again. She wanted to know whether Larry was coming home to repair the cabinet.

He told her he had been conducting an important technology demonstration. She asked whether the demonstration was finished.

"Almost." "Good. Bring your screwdriver."

He promised he would be home shortly.

Then, apparently determined to prove that the day had not been wasted, Larry asked the computer for a step-by-step guide to tightening a loose kitchen cabinet handle. The instructions appeared immediately: they advised him to inspect the screws, identify the appropriate screwdriver, tighten the hardware carefully, and replace damaged fasteners if necessary.

Larry looked pleased. "See, Don? That's exactly what I'm talking about. It makes everything easier." I asked how long the repair would take. "Probably five minutes." "How long have you been putting it off?" "About three weeks."

Frank stood up. "Well, there's your technological breakthrough. The computer has finally convinced you to do something your wife told you to do three weeks ago."

Larry packed his laptop and left.

About twenty minutes later, he called me from his kitchen: he had tightened the handle, but one screw had been stripped and needed replacing. He wanted to know whether I had a spare. I told him to check his garage. He said he had already looked. I asked whether he had tried asking the computer where he kept his screws, but he did not appreciate that suggestion.

Frank, who was still sitting in my kitchen, offered to bring over a small box of assorted hardware. He had the right screw, and the repair was completed before Helen finished preparing dinner.

Later, Helen sent me a photograph of the cabinet with the handle properly attached. Beneath it, she had written: "Three weeks, one webinar, two computer-generated messages, and Frank's screwdriver. Progress."

I showed Frank. He said Helen ought to be the neighborhood's technology consultant.

By Sunday morning, Larry had sent me another message. This one contained a short essay about how artificial intelligence could help communities adapt to economic change. He had clearly spent part of the evening thinking about our conversation.

I read it over coffee. Some of the points were reasonable: AI can make useful information easier to obtain and reduce time spent on repetitive tasks; it can also make mistakes, produce confident answers that are wrong, and create new problems when people rely on it without checking the results. Employers have legitimate reasons to explore tools that improve productivity, and workers have equally legitimate reasons to ask how those improvements will affect their employment, wages, and opportunities.

The difficult part is that nobody can tell every worker exactly how the next several years will unfold. Some occupations will change substantially, some tasks may disappear, and other kinds of work may grow. The effects will depend on the technology, the industry, the decisions employers make, and whether workers have meaningful opportunities to adapt. Anybody who claims to know precisely how many jobs will exist ten years from now is making a prediction, not reporting a settled fact.

I don't object to machines doing work that people would rather not do. If a computer can help a nurse spend less time on paperwork and more time with patients, that sounds useful; if it helps a small business owner prepare an invoice without staying up until midnight, I can appreciate that; and if it assists somebody learning a new skill or navigating a complicated task, there is value in that too.

What concerns me is how casually some people discuss the workers who might be displaced. They speak about retraining as though a person can simply put a twenty-year career in a cardboard box, enroll in a course, and emerge three months later with a new profession, a comparable salary, and no interruption in mortgage payments. Some people will make those transitions successfully; others will need time, financial support, and opportunities that may not be available where they live.

I thought about Frank's cousin, who had to find another job after his warehouse changed its operations. I thought about the people who answer phones, prepare reports, process documents, and perform the thousands of ordinary tasks that keep businesses functioning. I wondered how many of them were being invited into conversations about the technology that might change their work.

Then I thought about Larry. He had spent most of Saturday demonstrating a system that could prepare meal plans, compose messages, organize schedules, and draft impressive applications, yet the most useful thing he accomplished all weekend was tightening a cabinet handle with a screwdriver borrowed from Frank.

I called him to ask how the cabinet was holding up.

"Perfectly," he said. "Good. Did you thank Frank?" "Of course." "Did you thank the computer?"

He laughed. "Don, you're never going to let me forget this, are you?" "Not while the cabinet's still attached."

He told me he was considering another webinar, this one about how AI could help people prepare for future careers. I said that sounded interesting and asked whether he planned to attend.

"Absolutely." "What time?" "Saturday morning."

I told him I would be busy.

"Doing what?" "Trying to enjoy a world in which I can still make breakfast without a consultant."

He laughed again and said I would eventually come around.

Perhaps I will. I have been wrong about technology before, and I expect to be wrong again. I once thought nobody needed a telephone they could carry everywhere; now I use one to check the weather, read the news, and discover that Larry has sent me another document.

But I still think the people celebrating a future in which machines do more of the work ought to spend a little more time explaining what happens to the people whose work the machines replace. That seems like a reasonable question to ask before declaring the future a complete success.

As for Larry, he sent me one final message Sunday evening: he wanted to know whether I would help him organize a neighborhood workshop titled Preparing for the AI-Powered Future.

I asked who would be teaching it. He said he would, with assistance from artificial intelligence.

I asked whether the computer knew it had been hired. Larry said that wasn't how the technology worked.

I told him he should probably ask it anyway: given everything we had heard about computers taking people's jobs, I thought it deserved to know that Larry was planning to take credit for its work.

He has not replied. I suspect he's preparing a presentation.

Until next time, Cranky DJ

Collected full article body: Finland’s next general election has been set for next April 18, hopefully bringing an end to the National Coalition Party’s current slash-and-burn coalition, in which the far-right Finns Party plays a key role. Recent polls have, however, seen the latter worryingly rise to second position, becoming the main right-wing force for the first time ever. Trailing Antti Lindtman’s Social Democrats (SDP) by 6 percentage points, the Finns Party is placing its hope in polarizing the election over immigration. Musculoskeletal ultrasound interpretation often demands specialized sonographic proficiency, creating substantial variability during routine disease monitoring. Investigators developed a deep learning platform designed to automate the detection of synovitis, power-Doppler signals, bone erosions, and osteophytes on sonographic scans. Clinicians highlight that preserving transparent reasoning, objective validation, and the central physician-patient relationship remains paramount as innovative platforms enter clinical practice.

Original headline: Pennsylvania Enacts Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act: New Disclosure Requirements for AI-Generated Advertising
English normalization: Pennsylvania Enacts Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act: New Disclosure Requirements for AI-Generated Advertising
Full article body: Pennsylvania has enacted legislation imposing new disclosure requirements on certain advertisements that use artificial intelligence (AI)-generated or AI-modified content. Senate Bill 806, now Act 99 of 2026, was signed into law by Governor Josh Shapiro on October 22, 2026. The statute, titled the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act, establishes a disclosure requirement for advertisers whose use of synthetic content creates a false consumer perception about the nature, origin, or authenticity of the goods or services being advertised.

The law is particularly relevant to businesses that use AI-generated images, videos, or audio in their marketing and advertising campaigns, including financial services providers that employ synthetic content to promote lending products, deposit accounts, payment services, or other consumer financial products. Although the statute is directed at deceptive advertising rather than AI use generally, its broad definitions and disclosure requirements warrant attention from businesses using generative AI in consumer-facing advertising.

What Does the New Law Require?

Section 4 prohibits an advertiser from creating and disseminating, or causing the creation and dissemination of, an advertisement using synthetic content in a manner that creates a false consumer perception about the nature, origin, or authenticity of the advertised goods or services, unless the advertisement includes a clear and conspicuous disclosure that the content was modified or generated using AI.

The statute defines “synthetic content” as information, including an image, video, audio clip, or text, that has been significantly modified or generated by AI. Its definition of AI expressly includes generative AI.

The law does not impose a blanket disclosure requirement whenever an advertiser uses AI. Rather, the disclosure obligation is tied to the use of synthetic content in a manner that creates a false consumer perception about the advertised goods or services.

For example, an advertiser using an AI-generated video that appears to depict a real customer describing an actual experience with a financial product could face questions under the statute if the presentation creates a false impression about the authenticity of the testimonial. Similarly, synthetic audio or imagery that falsely suggests a product, service, or endorsement is genuine could trigger the disclosure requirement.

Whether a particular advertisement falls within the statute will depend on its content, context, and presentation.

What Constitutes a Clear and Conspicuous Disclosure?

The statute imposes detailed requirements governing the placement and presentation of disclosures. A disclosure must satisfy the following requirements:

- Noticeability and comprehension. The disclosure must be presented in a size, color, contrast, location, duration, and audibility that make it readily noticeable, readable, understandable, and capable of being heard.

- Language. The disclosure must be presented in the language or other form of interaction the consumer uses to interact with or comprehend the synthetic content.

- Consistency. The disclosure cannot contradict or be inconsistent with other information presented alongside it.

- Proximity. When the disclosure modifies, explains, or clarifies other information, it must appear sufficiently close to that information to be noticed and understood, and it cannot be obscured.

- Audio and visual presentation. Audio disclosures must be delivered at a volume and cadence sufficient for consumers to hear and comprehend them. Visual disclosures must be sufficiently legible and remain on screen long enough for consumers to read and understand them.

- Print advertisements. Disclosures in print advertisements and promotional materials, including point-of-sale displays and brochures, must be sufficiently noticeable and use type that contrasts with the background.

The statute also requires the disclosure to appear the first time the synthetic content is presented to the consumer, in the same medium as the synthetic content, and, to the extent technically feasible, in a form that is permanent or extraordinarily difficult to remove.

These requirements make the manner of disclosure as important as its substance. A disclosure that is technically present but difficult to see, hear, or understand may not satisfy the statute.

Exceptions

The statute excludes three categories of content from its disclosure requirement:

- Content that is evidently fictional based on the content or context of the depiction.

- Parody, satire, commentary, or criticism.

- Content limited to text.

The text-only exception is notable. Although the statute’s definition of synthetic content encompasses text significantly modified or generated by AI, the disclosure provision expressly excludes content limited to text. Consequently, AI-generated text alone does not trigger this particular disclosure requirement, even though other laws governing deceptive advertising may remain applicable.

The exception for evidently fictional content also suggests that the law is principally concerned with synthetic depictions that could mislead consumers into believing that an advertisement or its underlying representation is authentic. The statute does not, however, define a specific test for determining when content is evidently fictional.

Enforcement and Potential Penalties

The Attorney General or appropriate district attorney may also bring a civil action for violations. A court may award a civil fine of up to $3,000, as well as actual attorney fees and court costs.

The statute does not expressly create a private right of action. Its enforcement provisions identify the Attorney General and appropriate district attorneys as the officials authorized to bring actions under the Act. The provision authorizing a court to award damages does not, standing alone, resolve every question concerning who may pursue a claim, but the text does not expressly authorize consumers to sue directly under the new law.

Importantly, the Act provides that disclosure of AI use does not limit any other recourse available under law. Thus, compliance with the new disclosure requirement does not immunize an advertiser from otherwise applicable claims based on deceptive advertising or other unlawful conduct.

Implications for Consumer Financial Services Providers

Banks, credit unions, finance companies, fintechs, payment providers, and other consumer-facing businesses should evaluate their use of synthetic content in advertising distributed in Pennsylvania.

The most immediate concern is not the use of AI itself, but the potential for synthetic content to create a misleading impression about a product, service, customer experience, endorsement, or other material representation. Advertisers should consider whether their campaigns include AI-generated or materially AI-modified testimonials, spokespersons, product demonstrations, audio, or video.

Businesses should consider taking the following steps:

- Review consumer-facing advertisements that use AI-generated or significantly AI-modified images, videos, and audio.

- Determine whether the content could create a false impression about the nature, origin, or authenticity of the advertised goods or services.

- Establish a process for including disclosures in the same medium as the synthetic content, beginning with its first presentation.

Businesses should also distinguish this law’s specific disclosure obligation from their broader compliance obligations. The Act does not authorize deceptive advertising merely because an advertiser discloses the use of AI, nor does it establish a general safe harbor for AI-generated marketing.

Effective Date

The Act provides that it takes effect 60 days after enactment. Because Governor Shapiro approved it on October 22, 2026, the new requirements are scheduled to take effect on December 21, 2026.

Takeaway

Pennsylvania’s Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act adds another state-level requirement to the evolving legal framework governing the use of generative AI in commercial communications. Its scope is narrower than a general AI transparency mandate: the disclosure requirement applies to specified uses of synthetic content that create a false consumer perception about advertised goods or services, subject to the statute’s stated exceptions.

Nevertheless, businesses using AI-generated imagery, audio, or video in consumer advertising should not assume that a disclosure buried in fine print or added after the content has already been presented will suffice. Reviewing advertising practices and implementing appropriate disclosure controls before the December 21 effective date would be a prudent compliance measure.

Publisher: En attendant Nadeau
Date: 2026-11-03T21:16:14+00:00
Source language: fr
Original headline: Intelligence artificielle & nouveau fascisme, de Rainer Mühlhoff : Gouverner sans être contredit
English normalization: Artificial Intelligence & New Fascism, by Rainer Mühlhoff: Governing Without Being Challenged
Full article body: Dans Intelligence artificielle & nouveau fascisme, le philosophe Rainer Mühlhoff explore les manières dont nos démocraties utilisent l’IA, les risques majeurs que ces usages font porter sur nos systèmes politiques et nos libertés. Pour conjurer cette pente fasciste dangereuse, il fait des propositions concrètes et utiles.

« Imaginons que, dans une agence pour l’emploi, nous dirigions un service chargé de décider… » Rainer Mühlhoff place au cœur de son essai une expérience de pensée d’apparence modeste. Le service doit dire s’il suspend les indemnités d’un chômeur qui a quitté son emploi, et il peut s’y prendre de deux façons. Dans la première procédure, des agents examinent chaque dossier : démission volontaire, contrat arrivé à son terme, harcèlement, maladie… Cette voie est lente et coûteuse, mais chaque étape peut être retracée, contrôlée par sondage, reprise par le juge. Dans la seconde, des agents chevronnés décident à l’intuition, de façon que la décision ait « de fortes chances de passer » ; une prime récompense ceux dont les décisions ne sont pas contestées, une retenue frappe ceux dont on annule trop souvent les décisions. Le premier service examine, le second parie. C’est ce second service, explique l’auteur, qu’une intelligence artificielle fait tourner sans personnel supplémentaire, à n’importe quelle échelle.

Mathématicien de formation, docteur en philosophie, Mühlhoff enseigne l’éthique de l’IA à l’université d’Osnabrück. Son livre a reçu en Allemagne le prix du livre politique de la fondation Friedrich-Ebert. Sa thèse tient en une phrase : le fascisme à l’ère de l’IA est « le moment historique où la préemption fondée sur l’IA, la violence étatique et des idéologies anti-égalitaires se condensent en un projet étatique explicitement antidémocratique ». L’essai descend par couches, du fonctionnement des machines aux discours de leurs promoteurs, puis à leur radicalisation politique, jusqu’au DOGE d’Elon Musk et aux opérations de la police de l’immigration à Minneapolis en janvier 2026. Il refuse deux facilités : le déterminisme, qui ferait de l’IA une machine à fabriquer du fascisme, et la lecture « purement instrumentale », qui ne verrait dans l’alliance des patrons de la tech et de l’alt-right qu’une affaire de profits.

Le lecteur pressé de rejoindre l’actualité américaine aurait tort de sauter le deuxième chapitre, qui est le cœur du livre. Les systèmes de classification probabiliste qu’étudie Mühlhoff ne disent rien, selon lui, du cas particulier : ils le classent d’après sa ressemblance avec des cas déjà connus. Transposée dans l’administration, cette logique change la nature de la vérité, qui devient une « valeur procédurale » : il s’agit de « pacifier » le plus grand nombre de cas au moindre coût, de décider « de manière à ce qu’il y ait le moins de contestations possible ». Dans le service imaginé par l’auteur, le système n’apprend ses erreurs que par les recours. Or ceux qui contestent le moins sont ceux qui en ont le moins les moyens : leurs erreurs ne remontent pas, le modèle les reproduit, et l’injustice s’accumule là où l’on se défend mal, jusqu’à fabriquer des écarts entre groupes qu’il prétendait seulement mesurer. C’est le modèle d’une administration qui ne cherche plus la décision juste, mais celle qui passera, et pour laquelle le silence des administrés vaut approbation.

Mühlhoff ne prétend pas que cette administration attende le fascisme pour exister. « Il est certes possible d’utiliser l’IA dans l’administration sans compromettre les principes de l’État de droit », écrit-il, avant de citer en note l’Espagne et les Pays-Bas comme exemples d’usages irresponsables. Le cas néerlandais éclaire pourtant ce que le livre laisse en suspens. De 2013 à 2019, l’administration fiscale a confié à un modèle auto-apprenant le choix des demandes d’allocations de garde d’enfants à contrôler de plus près, et, au moins de mars 2016 à octobre 2018, la nationalité entrait dans son calcul du risque. Une législation rigide, interprétée de la manière la plus sévère, permettait alors de réclamer toute une année d’allocations pour une irrégularité mineure. La commission d’enquête parlementaire impute le désastre à cette application plus qu’au seul modèle, et elle met en cause le juge : la justice administrative a, selon elle, « contribué de manière substantielle » pendant des années à une rigueur que la loi n’imposait pas. Les recours s’étaient multipliés, deux journalistes, de Trouw et de RTL Nieuws, avaient révélé l’usage de fausses preuves, et des députés réclamaient des comptes lorsque le Conseil d’État a rompu, en octobre 2019, avec sa ligne du « tout ou rien ». Deux ans plus tard, il présentait ses excuses aux parents : « Nous aurions pu et dû changer plus tôt notre ligne sévère. » En Australie, le dispositif Robodebt, qui calculait sans IA des dettes sociales à partir de revenus moyennés, n’a été suspendu qu’en novembre 2019, quelques jours avant que l’État reconnaisse son illégalité devant un tribunal.

Ces précédents ne réfutent pas Mühlhoff ; ils déplacent l’épreuve de sa thèse. Dans son expérience de pensée, les contrôles existent, les recours demeurent, le juge intervient, et son dernier chapitre convoque journalistes et fonctionnaires. Le cas néerlandais révèle que ces garanties peuvent cohabiter des années durant avec une injustice massive, et que le juge lui-même peut en devenir l’un des rouages. Préserver les voies de recours ne suffit donc pas : il faut savoir pourquoi elles échouent, et à quelles conditions elles corrigent.

On mesure alors ce que la conjoncture américaine a de neuf. Mühlhoff cite Russell Vought, directeur du budget de Donald Trump : « Nous voulons que les bureaucrates soient traumatisés. » Les actes ont suivi, et ils visent les organes de contrôle eux-mêmes : dix-sept inspecteurs généraux, chargés de détecter les abus dans les administrations fédérales, ont été congédiés en une soirée de janvier 2025, sans le préavis que la loi exige. En février, Vought, devenu directeur par intérim du Bureau de protection financière des consommateurs, y faisait cesser toute supervision. À Minneapolis, des milliers d’agents fédéraux, guidés par des drones, des lecteurs de plaques et des croisements de fichiers, ont traqué les migrants pendant des semaines. Les mécanismes de protection constitutionnels, écrit Mühlhoff, « bien que maintenus dans la forme », y perdaient leur capacité à limiter un pouvoir armé.

Les démocraties ont montré qu’un État peut se tromper à grande échelle sans verser dans le fascisme ; le danger propre à cette conjoncture est qu’un pouvoir s’emploie à neutraliser ceux qui pourraient établir ses erreurs, tandis que ses moyens de classer et de contraindre se déploient. Le livre décrit les conditions dans lesquelles ces deux mouvements pourraient se renforcer : centralisation des données, dépendance envers des infrastructures privées, État devenu, selon la juriste Hannah Ruschemeier qu’il cite, à la fois détenteur du pouvoir de l’IA et chargé d’en corriger les effets. Il reste plus difficile de savoir jusqu’où cette convergence est déjà réalisée, et l’auteur passe souvent du constat à l’anticipation : « on peut s’attendre à une fusion du pouvoir étatique et du pouvoir de la tech ». Entre le pari du deuxième chapitre et l’identification d’une personne par une police de l’immigration, quels dispositifs et quelles chaînes de responsabilité établissent le passage ?

La généalogie des « idéologies de la tech », de l’eugénisme de Julian Huxley au long-termisme, de Curtis Yarvin à J. D. Vance, fait apparaître des conceptions du progrès qui légitiment les hiérarchies humaines et, chez Yarvin, un pouvoir pensé sur le modèle de l’entreprise, jusqu’à la « monarchie du PDG ». Mühlhoff n’ignore pas les intérêts : il voit dans ces visions d’un avenir lointain « des contributions politiques cherchant à imposer certains intérêts dans le présent ». Il examine moins les divergences entre des courants dont les doctrines, les intérêts et les positions sur la régulation ne coïncident pas toujours. À l’été 2024, un projet de loi californien encadrant les modèles d’IA les plus puissants était défendu par des proches de l’« altruisme efficace », combattu notamment par le fonds Andreessen Horowitz, et soutenu par Elon Musk. Un désaccord sur une loi laisse subsister une convergence plus large ; il oblige pourtant à demander si l’idéologie commune suffit à expliquer l’alliance, au-delà des intérêts et des occasions du moment.

Sur le calcul probabiliste lui-même, l’histoire de l’État social offre un repère. La loi de 1898 sur les accidents du travail remplace la quête de la faute patronale par un principe de réparation fondé sur le risque professionnel ; François Ewald y voit un moment fondateur de l’État-providence. Ce qui distingue l’usage que décrit Mühlhoff n’est donc pas la probabilité elle-même, mais la destination qu’on lui donne : servir à organiser la prise en charge collective d’un risque, ou à l’imputer à chacun.

Le livre se clôt sur un programme : isoler les forces antidémocratiques, défendre les institutions de l’intérieur, réguler davantage, l’Union européenne en tête. L’Union a bien inscrit dans son règlement sur l’IA un droit à l’explication de certaines décisions individuelles, qui couvre l’attribution des prestations sociales ; elle vient aussi de reporter à décembre 2027 les principales obligations applicables à ces systèmes. Rendre une décision révisable ne se réduit pas à ouvrir un guichet de réclamation à qui n’en connaît ni les critères, ni les données, ni parfois l’existence. Il y faut des motifs accessibles, des données que l’on peut rectifier, des enquêteurs indépendants capables d’ouvrir la machine, et une autorité qui ait le pouvoir de l’arrêter. Les Pays-Bas l’ont appris aux dépens de plus de quarante mille parents reconnus lésés : la correction d’une injustice administrative ne peut reposer sur les seules personnes qu’elle frappe, ni sur des institutions qu’aucune autre ne vient éprouver. Mühlhoff demande aux journalistes, aux fonctionnaires et aux juges de défendre leurs institutions ; l’exemple néerlandais rappelle qu’il faut parfois les protéger contre leurs propres routines. Le danger commence quand une société perd les moyens de savoir qu’elle se trompe.

Full article body: Washington, D.C., 3 November 2026 (PAHO) - A total of 95 surveillance and public health professionals from 16 countries of the Americas participated in a series of training sessions organized by the Department of Health Emergencies of the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) to strengthen the use of the Epidemic Intelligence from Open Sources (EIOS) system. This platform makes it possible to identify and analyse signals of potential public health threats on the basis of information available in open sources.

The activities carried out between 6 and 29 October 2026 were aimed both at expanding the number of professionals trained in the use of EIOS and at incorporating new artificial intelligence-based functionalities to improve the detection and management of signals relevant for public health.

Early detection is essential to prevent health threats from becoming emergencies of greater magnitude. In this context, the use of digital tools such as EIOS makes it possible to complement traditional epidemiological surveillance systems through the systematic monitoring of open sources, facilitating the identification of signals that require verification and, where appropriate, a timely response by health authorities.

Capacity strengthening in 16 countries

Professionals from Costa Rica, Dominica, Guatemala, Jamaica, Mexico, Nicaragua, Peru and Uruguay participated in the training sessions on the main functions and tools of EIOS, aimed at facilitating their use in national event-based surveillance activities.

Specialized sessions on new artificial intelligence-based functionalities were also held. Representatives from Argentina, Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, El Salvador, Panama, Paraguay and the Dominican Republic participated in these sessions.

Greater capacities for timely early warning

These activities are part of PAHO's technical cooperation to strengthen epidemic intelligence and event-based surveillance in the countries of the Americas, within the framework of the Regional Action Plan for the strategy on epidemic intelligence for strengthening early warning of health emergencies 2024–2029, approved by the Member States of PAHO.

Through these actions, PAHO reaffirms its commitment to supporting countries in strengthening early warning systems that are more sensitive, timely and effective, capable of transforming available information into useful knowledge to anticipate risks and guide decisions that protect the health of the populations of the Americas.

Original headline: L’intelligence artificielle fait son entrée dans le réseau de la santé

Full article body: Fonctionnel dans la Capitale-Nationale et les Laurentides depuis la fin du mois de septembre, l’assistant virtuel vise à réduire les temps d’attente au 811, tout en aidant les infirmières dans leur quotidien.

Le fonctionnement est simple. Un patient qui souhaite consulter pour un problème de santé non urgent peut maintenant se rendre sur le site 811.sante.quebec.

Il remplit d’abord un court formulaire avec son identité, son numéro de téléphone, ses antécédents et sa médication, puis discute avec un assistant virtuel, par écrit ou à voix haute.

L’intelligence artificielle lui pose les questions qu’une infirmière poserait au début d’un appel concernant la raison de la consultation, l’intensité du problème et ses symptômes. À la fin, elle montre un résumé simple pour que le patient confirme que tout est exact.

Transféré à une infirmière

Les informations sont ensuite transférées à une infirmière d’Info-Santé, qui rappelle l’individu.

Après avoir validé le formulaire produit par l’IA, elle peut passer directement à l’étape de l’évaluation. L’intelligence artificielle lui propose également quelques «pistes de vigilance» à prendre en considération.

Pendant sa conversation avec le patient, l’infirmière ajoute manuellement des notes qu’elle juge pertinentes. Le résumé est ensuite envoyé aux médecins qui assureront le suivi du dossier, évitant ainsi au patient de répéter son histoire lors de consultations futures.

Déjà des résultats

Marie-Eve Brunelle, directrice des soins primaires intégrés à Santé Québec, pilote le développement de ce projet.

L’assistant virtuel a vu le jour pour répondre à un besoin qui avait été nommé par les équipes sur le terrain, dit-elle : réduire les délais d’attente à Info-Santé. Et il fait déjà ses preuves.

Entre le 29 septembre et le 27 octobre, le temps moyen de traitement d’un appel 811 dans les centrales accueillant les projets pilotes a diminué de 23 %. Il est passé de 29 minutes et 38 secondes à 22 minutes et 49 secondes, ce qui représente un gain de près de 7 minutes.

Full article body: - Published

Some EU rules on Artificial Intelligence (AI) will apply in Northern Ireland, the UK government has said.

However the regulation of AI in NI will largely be a matter for the UK government and Stormont.

EU rules will only apply to physical goods which have an embedded AI system.

They will apply due to the Windsor Framework, the Brexit deal which keeps NI inside the EU's single market for goods.

The EU's AI Act was passed in 2024 and in 2025 the European Commission proposed that the parts concerning goods should apply in NI. That has been under negotiation with the UK since then.

The government said: "The EU AI Act does not apply to NI in full. It applies only where an AI system is closely integrated with a tangible physical product that is placed on the NI market.

"It would not affect an NI business simply because it uses online or downloadable AI tools to manage work, analyse data, or carry out business functions.

"It would also not place obligations on the developers of those tools for their use in NI, unless the AI is closely integrated into a physical product placed on the NI market."

The Cabinet Office minister Hamish Falconer said the addition of the AI rules to the Windsor Framework would not create a new regulatory border with the rest of the UK.

"The regulation will mainly apply to physical products in scope of the Windsor Framework, that already adhere to EU law," he said it a written statement to parliament.

"This provides Northern Ireland manufacturers certainty on their unique dual market access to the EU market and the rest of the UK market."

Falconer added that the government's assessment was that "products subject to prohibitions or high-risk requirements are currently relatively rare, and that in any case, businesses supplying NI in many affected sectors are typically EU-facing meaning they will comply with EU law requirements".

Examples of products which will be covered by the EU laws include a smart speaker with a built-in AI voice assistant or a smart watch requiring a manufacturer's AI health monitoring app.

The main idea of the EU law is to regulate AI based on its capacity to cause harm to society. The higher the risk, the stricter the rules with some AI applications being banned.

The government's examples of some physical products which could be banned include "a connected toy embedding AI that encourages children to undertake increasingly risky activities in exchange for reward or praise" or "an AI-connected camera with voice recognition that detects employee emotions , external."

In general terms when the EU's rules on the regulation of goods are updated the UK government has to agree which of them should apply in NI.

In some circumstances the NI Assembly also has a vote on the matter.

De plus en plus de Français affirment utiliser l'intelligence artificielle (IA) pour se rassurer autour de leur santé avant même d'avoir consulté un médecin. 50 % des Français utilisent désormais cet assistant pour leur santé d'après les résultats du baromètre Acsel et Toluna publié cette semaine. Un taux en hausse de 5 points par rapport à l'année précédente.

Parmi les interrogés, certains avouent faire des recherches via l'intelligence artificielle avant ou après avoir consulté un médecin. Les soignants en ont déjà mesuré les effets. 38% des soignants ont déjà vu un patient contester leur diagnostic ou demander des précisions après un échange avec une IA. Pour quelques sondés, l'assistant remplace même le docteur.

À 41 ans, Pauline utilise l'intelligence artificielle pour sa santé et celle de ses trois enfants.

"Dès qu'il y a un petit symptôme, quelque chose qui peut m'inquiéter, je regarde sur Google. Avec l'IA sur ChatGPT, je peux lui demander de faire une petite description et avoir un premier avis, pour doser s'il y a une espèce d'urgence"

, admet-elle. D'autres comme Emma, pensent que l'IA peut compléter une consultation pour ne pas passer à côté de certains symptômes :

"Les médecins aujourd'hui sont pressés par le temps. Je pense que cela peut apporter un angle qui n'est pas vu peut-être sur le moment car on est pris par le patient d'avant, on ne pose pas toutes les questions"

.

Selon ce baromètre, l'intelligence artificielle est même devenue un réflexe, notamment en ce qui concerne la santé mentale. 30 % des Français affirment l'avoir déjà utilisée pour une question psychologique, d'après les conclusions du baromètre.

"Il m'a dit, 'j'ai peut-être ça, qu'est-ce que vous en pensez ?'"

Pour Nicolas de Chanaud médecin généraliste chez Ipso santé à Paris, se renseigner en amont d'une consultation n'est pas vraiment un phénomène nouveau :

"Cela fait des années que les patients vont regarder des sites en passant par Google ou un équivalent. Ils viennent nous voir et nous disent, 'moi Google, il m'a dit que j'ai peut-être ça, qu'est-ce que vous en pensez ?'"

Aujourd'hui, cela va plus loin, selon le médecin.

"Ils vont interroger un outil d'intelligence artificielle, par exemple ChatGPT et la grosse différence, c'est que l'outil va leur donner un avis, mais il va être assez sûr de lui"

, constate Nicolas de Chanaud.

D'après lui, ChatGPT n'a pas forcément tout faux mais il est important de se souvenir qu'il propose juste une solution. "

Moi, je vais poser des questions à mon patient pour explorer cette solution. Je vais l'examiner, je vais peut-être lui prescrire des examens complémentaires pour justement essayer d'étayer ou pas cette hypothèse de l'intelligence artificielle"

, explique-t-il.

Du côté des soignants, ils ont pour certains complètement intégré l'IA dans leur quotidien. 43 % l'utilisent chaque jour d'après le baromètre et près d'un tiers des médecins déclare avoir déjà modifié une décision clinique après avoir effectué des recherches grâce à l'intelligence artificielle.

Original headline: L’intelligence artificielle déjà indispensable pour gagner les 24 Heures du Mans ?
English normalization: Is Artificial Intelligence Already Indispensable to Win the 24 Hours of Mansfield?
Full article body: C’est le couteau suisse des temps modernes. Comme une version infinie du célèbre outil à tout faire helvète, l’intelligence artificielle est en train de bouleverser le début du XXIe siècle par un développement accéléré et généralisé. On ne peut déjà plus s’en passer.

La Genesis GMR-001 est l’unique nouveauté de l’année dans la catégorie Hypercar. Quelle part a pris l’intelligence artificielle dans la conception de cette nouvelle voiture de course, plutôt 5 % ou 50 % ? Une petite part, d’après François-Xavier Demaison, le directeur technique de l’équipe coréenne : « C’est encore difficile à appliquer à l’aérodynamique, au niveau où est aujourd’hui l’endurance, mais cela fait partie des éléments à développer, un axe qu’on va devoir travailler. […] On l’utilise en rallye, on va forcément l’utiliser ici. » Le Français se montre évasif quant aux freins à l’utilisation de l’IA. En effet, pour faire analyser des données par un moteur d’intelligence artificielle, il faut les lui confier. Il y a là un enjeu de confidentialité qui, dans l’état actuel des choses, semble être un vrai point de blocage pour certaines équipes engagées aux 24 Heures du Mans. Ingénieur de piste de l’Oreca 07 #14 TDS Racing en catégorie LMP2, Arthur Trouttet concède ainsi : « On ne s’en sert pas assez, pour être honnête, mais on s’y met. Pour l’instant, on n’a pas dans notre équipe quelque chose qui est en lien direct avec l’IA. Mais on s’en sert dans la phase de préparation. »

“Aujourd’hui, on n’a pas encore trouvé l’IA qui va nous dessiner une voiture, mais on va y travailler.”

— François-Xavier Demaison, directeur technique Genesis Magma Racing

Cinq fois vainqueure des 24 Heures du Mans, l’équipe Toyota Racing est autonome dans le domaine, nous confie David Floury, directeur technique de Toyota Racing : « On utilise différentes plateformes qui existent, mais on a également la compétence en interne et un département entier dédié à l’intelligence artificielle. Depuis quatre ou cinq ans, le développement est exponentiel. En premier lieu, on s’en sert pour la transcription en direct des réunions qui, chez nous, sont multilingues. C’est capital, parce que Toyota Racing est très multiculturelle et que nous faisons des meetings entre le Japon, l’Europe, et avec les différentes entités de Toyota dans le monde. C’est un premier aspect, mais sur les aspects techniques, on voit aussi une évolution très rapide. »

L’intelligence artificielle sera-t-elle capable de concevoir une Hypercar de A à Z ? Sans aucun doute. Mais quand ?

« On n’a pas encore essayé, donc je ne peux pas répondre à cette question. En revanche, je peux vous dire que, si on demande à des moteurs d’intelligence artificielle d’analyser un règlement, ils ont une capacité de synthèse et d’analyse des éléments de règlementation – sportive comme technique – qui est assez surprenante. On n’en est pas encore à concevoir une voiture en utilisant uniquement l’intelligence artificielle, mais je pense que l’hypothèse que cela arrive dans le futur n’est pas irréaliste. » À quel point la nouvelle Toyota TR010 Hybrid bénéficie-t-elle des possibilités offertes par l’intelligence artificielle ? On ne le saura pas, mais une chose est certaine, c’est que toutes les voitures de course en contiennent une dose.

Une fois la voiture sur la piste, l’IA se montre encore indispensable. « Elle nous sert à analyser rapidement un volume de données important. Ce n’est pas encore un outil de prise de décision à 100 % ; par contre, c’est un élément qui aide à la stratégie, à la tactique, en termes de capacité d’analyse. »

Alors à quoi faut-il s’attendre dans les années à venir ? « À tous niveaux, que ce soit dans la conception, le développement de la voiture, l’exploitation ou la stratégie, cela va continuer à s’accélérer et devenir de plus en plus prégnant, partout, dans tous les domaines », conclut David Floury pour l’équipe Toyota Racing.

Alors que la Cour européenne des droits de l'homme (CEDH) croule sous les demandes et est souvent critiquée pour la lenteur de ses procédures, son président voit dans l'IA générative un moyen d'accélérer le traitement des dossiers. Il est tout de même conscient que ces outils pourraient encore plus surcharger l'institution.

Une technologie sur laquelle il ne faut pas faire l'impasse.

Déjà utilisée dans le système judiciaire

, notamment pour la recherche de jurisprudence ou comme aide à la constitution d'un dossier, l'IA générative met la Cour européenne des droits de l'homme (CEDH)

devant "un nouveau défi"

, car elle l'expose à un risque accru de plaintes abusives, mais peut aussi accélérer le traitement des dossiers, résume son président, Matthias Guyomar.

"Si nous n'utilisons pas l'IA, nous serons mangés. Nous serons submergés. Et nous ne pourrons plus rendre la justice", prévient-il dans un entretien à l'AFP. "Nous savons très bien que nous pouvons peut-être demain avoir, en un clic, des milliers de requêtes générées par l'intelligence artificielle qui nous arrivent", pointe-t-il lors de cet entretien accordé mercredi, date anniversaire de la signature de la Convention européenne des droits de l'homme en 1950, que la CEDH est chargée d'appliquer dans les 46 pays membres.

Il faudra alors pouvoir détecter rapidement si "les requêtes sont abusives", poursuit Matthias Guyomar, soulignant l'exemple récent d'une plainte reçue "portant sur un cas complètement faux, inventé". Le phénomène reste marginal, mais "nous nous attendons à ce que cela se multiplie". Et si elles sont valides, la Cour devra "traiter cette masse d'affaires", souligne le Français, nommé en mai 2025 à la tête de l'institution pour un mandat de trois ans. Alors même que l'institution croule déjà sous les demandes et est souvent critiquée pour la lenteur de ses procédures.

Processus d'automatisation en cours

La CEDH, basée à Strasbourg, est l'instance de dernier recours pour les particuliers estimant que leurs droits ont été violés, après épuisement de toutes les procédures dans leur pays. L'an passé, la CEDH a réduit à 53.450 le total de ses affaires en cours, le plus bas niveau depuis 20 ans, grâce notamment à une augmentation de 5% des cas jugés.

Mais ce stock est remonté à plus de 60.000 cette année après un afflux de requêtes, particulièrement en provenance de Turquie, dans le sillage de la répression après la tentative de coup d'État de 2016.

La Cour a certes engagé un processus d'automatisation, avec un outil interne qui permet de faciliter les recherches en circuit fermé, et une aide à la traduction. Mais, il s'agit d'aller plus loin et de "voir dans quelles mesures nous pouvons le faire aussi dans le processus plus directement juridictionnel", souligne le magistrat. En préalable, la CEDH va élaborer une "charte éthique" dont l'adoption est prévue l'an prochain et qui sera rendue publique.

"Il y a une condition principielle, c'est que l'humain doit rester dans la boucle. Et qu'il n'est pas question de déléguer à la machine ce qui est proprement de l'ordre du délibéré judiciaire", tranche-t-il.

Mais cette intégration de l'IA aura un coût, et dépendra donc du bon vouloir des pays membres, alors même que les moyens manquent déjà selon lui. "Il faut avoir ça à l'esprit: nous avons une juridiction sur 700 millions de personnes, et l'année dernière, nous avons jugé 38.000 affaires" avec 46 juges et 650 membres du greffe, énumère-t-il. Tout cela avec un budget inférieur à 90 millions d'euros, dit-il: "ce n'est pas suffisant".
